en: The *Samāsasūtra*:
The *Sarvopakāriṇī* Commentary.
That pure splendor of speech which fully awakens one to the stainless reality—the manifold and primordial reality—arising from the entire collection of stainless principles.
I bow with reverence to that primordial Lord, the venerable Great Seer Kapila, who brings about the ultimate good for all worlds. // 1 //
Desiring to uplift [this work] so that the true meaning of the sūtras it presents may be understood,
and being submissive to virtue, I compose this commentary which is beneficial to all.

Then, desiring to uplift those who are helpless, wretched, and fallen into the ocean of beginningless afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the most compassionate Great Sage, the Blessed Lord Kapila—who possesses self-perfected knowledge of reality—taught twenty-two aphorisms (*sūtra*).
For the etymological derivation of *sūtra* is "that which indicates" (*sūcanāt*).
Consequently, by means of these, there is an indication of all the principles (*tattva*) as well as the entire meaning of the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*.
This [work] is the root of all Sāṃkhya traditions, while other traditions are merely its elaborations.

Regarding this, the elders maintain that the *Sūtra-ṣaḍadhyāyī* was composed by the great sage, the venerable Kapila, who was an incarnation of Vaiśvānara; however, these twenty-two *sūtras*, which serve as the seed for even that [larger work], were composed by the great sage, the venerable Kapila, who was an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa.

Therein, first, by means of the initial three aphorisms, he indicates the twenty-five principles (tattvas) which constitute the root of the entire phenomenal world: "The eight primary natures (prakṛtis). (Tats 1)
The sixteen transformations. // 2 //
The person. // 3 //
This is the meaning: according to the Sāṃkhya system, there are twenty-five principles (*tattvas*).

Among these, there are eight primal natures (*prakṛtis*): the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

Here, "being a nature" (*prakṛtitva*) consists in being the originator of other principles; therefore, although the seven principles beginning with the Great One are each transformations of their respective predecessors, there is no contradiction, as they conform to this definition.

The five sense organs, the five organs of action, the mind, and the five elements known as ether, air, fire, water, and earth— these sixteen are merely modifications (*vikāra*); they are only transformations and do not initiate other fundamental principles (*tattva*), according to the logical maxim that "every statement is restrictive" (*sāvadhāraṇa*).
The Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth principle (*tattva*). He is neither primordial nature (*prakṛti*) nor a transformation (*vikṛti*), because he is defined by being distinguished from them.

By this, it is also indicated that the Puruṣa differs from primordial nature and the other principles, which possess qualities such as insentience, mutability, and agency; and thus says the *Kārikā*: [Sāṅkhya Kārikā 10]
Root nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and evolved;
the group of sixteen is evolved only; and the person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolved.
Thus [it is said].
Now, one might object: "But many other objects, such as jars and cloths, are seen that are distinct from these; how, then, can their existence be accounted for? To this, he says:
"The movement of the three qualities" (Tats_4).

*Traiguṇya* is simply the three *guṇas*: *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. The remainder [of the meaning] is that their movement (*sañcāra*)—in the manner of the "neck of a mad pigeon" (*mattakapotakaṇṭha*), characterized by a transformation distinct at every moment—is constantly occurring. By this, it is shown that the root nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) consists of the three *guṇas*; and by the number three, which indicates their differentiation, the *guṇas* are understood to have mutually contradictory natures consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion. Furthermore, by the term "movement" (*sañcāra*), which implies moving together or proceeding correctly, their eternal coexistence is indicated.
Furthermore, there is mutual assistance among the principles according to their respective functions in producing the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

Consequently, the complete accomplishment and production of all objects—such as pots and cloth—from *prakṛti*, the *mahat* and other evolutes, and the gross elements, occurs solely through the transformation characterized by the three *guṇas*. This is not something previously non-existent, but rather the mere manifestation of that which already existed in the form of its subtle cause.
It should be understood that these doctrines— the transformation into a form capable of gross effects and the theory of the pervasion of existence (sadvyāptivāda)— are thus indicated.

But surely, since the gunas have the inherent nature of incessant transformation, there could never be a non-perception of the class of objects; consequently, dissolution would be impossible. To this, he says:
"Pratisañcara" (re-absorption). [Tattvasamāsasūtra 5]
Just as there is a transformation of the three guṇas that effects the process of creation, so too there is a contrary transformation during the process of reabsorption (pratisañcāra).

Thus, it is indicated that when each respective effect is dissolved into its own cause through retrogressive transformation, the state of equilibrium of the three-guṇa-prakṛti is indeed dissolution (pralaya).
And at that time, because of their identical transformation, there is no manifestation of distinctness; this is the intended meaning.
Now, in order to distinguish the pleasure, pain, and so forth of one who is being born, he first states their threefold nature through one [term]:
"Internal" (adhyātma). (Tattvasaṃgraha 6)

"Relating to the self" means *adhyātma*. That is twofold: physical and mental. The physical is caused by an imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*); the mental is caused by desire, anger, greed, delusion, envy, and the perception or non-perception of specific objects. Both of these are called *adhyātma* because they are to be accomplished through internal means.
He states the two external divisions with two [verses]:
"The objective" (adhibhūta). [Tattvasaṃgraha 7]
The meaning is that "with respect to the presiding deity" (adhibhūta) refers to beings such as humans, animals, birds, reptiles, and stationary objects.
The divine [aspect]. (Tats_8)
This is the cause for possession by yakṣas, rākṣasas, vināyakas, grahas, and so forth;
both of these are called "external" because they are to be accomplished through external means.

Now, one might ask: even though there exist many distinct objects, how can suffering arise for the person from them, given that he lacks a connection to them? Therefore, intending to describe the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for that [suffering], [the author] first states the five sensory cognitions (*buddhi*): "The five sensory cognitions" (Tattvasaṃgraha 9).

Those by which objects are perceived and known on all sides are the *abhibuddhayaḥ*, the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriyāṇi*), namely those called the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin, which perceive form, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
And with this, in order to demonstrate yoga by way of knowledge, he speaks of the organs of action (*karmendriyāṇi*):
"The five sources of action" (Tats_10).

The five sense organs are the sources of action; they are the origins or causes of the actions of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and procreating, and they are known as the voice, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.
By this [verse], the connection between each specific organ and its respective object through the mediation of those particular actions is indicated.

Now, determination, egoism, and volition are the specific functions (vṛtti) of the Great Principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and the mind (manas) respectively; since it is impossible to grasp objects through the doors of the senses without these, and because those [specific functions] have already been largely defined by the mention of the grasping of objects by them, he states their common function:
"The five vital airs" (Tattvasaṃgraha 11).

The five vital airs (vāyus), known as prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna, are the common functions of the mahat, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and the mind; they are the means for sustaining life. Among them, prāṇa functions in the tip of the nose, the heart, the navel, and the big toes; apāna functions in the throat, the back, the anus, the sides, and the generative organ;

samāna functions in the heart, the navel, and all the joints; udāna functions in the heart, the throat, the palate, the head, and the space between the eyebrows; and vyāna has a pervasive function throughout the entire body.
He states the application of the five:
"The five are the agents of action. (Tats_12)

The function of these [channels] is the respective conveying of food and water that have been consumed, as well as of the lymph, blood, and so forth; the meaning is that their very nature consists in this, since they are inferred solely on the basis of that [function]. // 12 //

Now, one might object: "Granted that the Puruṣa possesses the capacity for all objects of thought and great egoism through the medium of cognition and activity; however, since the Puruṣa is not subject to transformation, that [capacity] is not possible. To dispel this doubt, he says:
"Ignorance has five sections" (Tattvasamāsasūtra 13).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the manifestation of what is not-self as self, and it is the adversary of knowledge (*vidyā*); it consists of five stages (*parvan*), which are known as ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the will to live (*abhiniveśa*). Thus, whatever object is determined through the inversion of ignorance by egoism and the others—which share its nature—they become attached to it; consequently, the sense is that there is a connection with that [object] through a lack of discrimination from the Self. (13) Among the fifty varieties of the evolution of mental states (*pratyayasarga*), the five types of error (*viparyaya*) have been described. Now, he speaks of the twenty-eight types of incapacity (*aśakti*) among the specific [evolutions].
Incapacity is of twenty-eight kinds. (Tattvasaṃgraha 14)

The eleven impairments of the sense organs and the seventeen impairments of the intellect—these are called the incapacities (*aśakti*). The impairments of the sense organs are as follows: deafness, leprosy, blindness, numbness, and likewise loss of smell.

Dumbness, lameness, crippledness, impotence, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), and dullness—these are the nine obstructions to the intellect (*buddhi-vadha*). They arise from the reversal of the eight attainments (*siddhi*) and the nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*); thus, there are twenty-eight kinds of incapacity (*aśakti*). // 14 //
Since [the means] have been mentioned, he states [the results], contentment and attainment, in two [verses]:
"Contentment is ninefold" (Tattvasaṃgraha 15).
As it has been said:
"The internal [contentments] are four, known as those consisting of nature, means, time, and fortune;
the external are five, resulting from the cessation of objects; thus nine contentments have been declared."

The meaning of this is as follows: When someone instructs that "the direct realization of discrimination (*viveka-sākṣātkāra*) is indeed a transformation of *prakṛti*, and since *prakṛti* itself effects that, there is no need for the practice of meditation," the contentment therein is called *prakṛti-tuṣṭi*. Then, when it is instructed that "since *prakṛti* is common to all, the direct realization of discrimination does not arise from her alone; rather, it arises through renunciation (*pravrajyā*)," the resulting contentment is called *upādāna-tuṣṭi* (2). Furthermore, when it is instructed that "even renunciation produces discrimination only by respecting a specific period of time; enough with excessive fervor," the resulting contentment is called *kāla-tuṣṭi* (3).
"Discriminative discernment arises through fortune alone"—this is the contentment called "fortune" (4).
These four are said to be "internal" because they arise with reference to the Self as distinct from primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
As for the five objects—known as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—the perception of the defects in their acquisition, preservation, loss, enjoyment, and injury [is the fifth contentment].

Next, there are five forms of cessation (*uparama*), which are also types of detachment (*virati*). These arise when one possesses dispassion toward the non-self—namely, the Great Principle (*mahat*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth—which one mistakenly conceives of as the self; therefore, they are called "external. These nine, being the opposites of what was previously stated, together with the twenty-eight forms of incapacity (*aśakti*), total forty-two. Because they stand as obstacles to the perfections (*siddhi*), they are to be abandoned.
The accomplishment is eightfold. // 16 //

They are as follows: reasoning (*ūha*), oral instruction (*śabda*), study (*adhyayana*), the three types of removal of suffering (*duḥkhavighāta*), acquisition of friends (*suhṛtprāpti*), and generosity (*dāna*). These are the eight means of attainment (*siddhi*). Among these, the first is the failure to attain knowledge of reality through one's own reasoning in the absence of instruction. The second, called "oral instruction" (*śabda*), is the arising of knowledge upon hearing the recitation of another's treatise. The third is the knowledge of reality resulting from study. [The fourth] is by means of the removal of the threefold suffering—internal, celestial, and elemental.

When the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) has arisen, there are three types of accomplishments (*siddhi*): [the sixth] through the acquisition of a friend who possesses such knowledge; [the seventh] the accomplishment called "acquisition of a friend" when the knowledge of reality is attained through the acquisition of a friend; and [the eighth] the eighth [accomplishment] when the knower of reality is propitiated with wealth and other means. Here, it should be understood that among the three accomplishments consisting of the destruction of suffering, these are primary, while the others are secondary because they serve as their means.

Beginning with the five misconceptions and ending with the eight perfections, these constitute the objective creation (*pratyayasarga*). Among these, for those desiring the discriminative discernment (*anyatākhyāti*) between primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the self (*pratyaya*), the forty-two [misconceptions] at the beginning are to be abandoned, while the perfections are to be acquired; this is indicated by the very exposition of their essential natures. // 16 //
Having described the creation of the intellect (*pratyayasarga*), he now speaks of the creation of primordial nature (*prakṛtisarga*):
"The ten root-meanings" (Tattvasamāsa 17).

There are ten categories (*padārtha*) that are "rooted" (*mūlika*); they are called "rooted" because their root—the *prakṛti* and the *puruṣa*—exist as their substratum, or because their root—their own nature (*svabhāva*)—exists as their efficient cause (*prayojaka*). That is to say, they exist within both the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) and the *puruṣa*. Thus, the *Rājavārttika* states: [text follows].
The existence of the Pradhāna, its unity, its purposefulness, its distinctness,
its being for the sake of another, as well as its non-identity, disjunction, and conjunction.
The remaining mode of existence and non-agency are remembered as the ten fundamental meanings.

In this context, singularity, purposefulness, subservience to another, predominance, distinctness with respect to primordial nature (*prakṛti*), non-agency, plurality in the person (*puruṣa*), existence, conjunction, and disjunction of both;
as well as the residual function—the functioning of the qualities (*guṇas*) through the relationship of subordinate and principal in the gross and subtle bodies—[are enumerated].

Here, by defining the similarities and differences between primordial nature and the person, it is indicated that the knowledge of the two as distinct is the seed for the discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*) of the difference between nature and the person.
And thus, because these phenomena possess their respective intrinsic natures, they are designated by the conventional term "natural creation" (prakṛtisarga). // 17 //

Now, one might object: "Since all effects are accomplished by the intellect (buddhi) and the other faculties which consist of the three guṇas, what is the purpose of postulating a further primordial nature (prakṛti)? To this, he says: "The creation for the sake of grace" (Tattvasaṃgraha 18).

When the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties are to produce their own effects, such as the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), they require the assistance of Nature’s favor; otherwise, the intellect, being exhausted, would not be capable of producing the ego-sense. Thus, the meaning is that the entire creation is rooted in that very favor. This alone is called the "filling of Nature" (*prakṛtyāpūra*). Consequently, it is indicated that this creation proceeds from Nature alone—not from God, nor with Brahman as its material cause, nor without a cause, nor from Nature presided over by God.
He states the creation of the subtle elements:
"The creation of the elements is of fourteen kinds" (Tattvasaṃgraha 19).
The creation of beings (bhūtasarga) is of fourteen types, distinguished by the categories of divine, animal, and human.

It is as follows: the divine is eightfold, divided into the Brahma, Prajāpati, Indra, Pitṛ, Gandharva, Yakṣa, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca [orders]; the animal is fivefold, divided into domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, immobile beings, and reptiles;
and the human is of one kind. (19)
Now, surely the desire for the reality of liberation—which is the crest-jewel of human goals—is only possible when there is knowledge of the nature of bondage; therefore, he speaks of bondage itself:
"Bondage is threefold. (Tats 20)
Bondage, arising from erroneous knowledge of reality, is threefold:
natural (*prākṛta*), modified (*vaikṛta*), and personal (*dākṣiṇa*).
Among these, the worship of *prakṛti* with the notion that it is the Puruṣa is natural bondage.

Likewise, the worship of the elements, the senses, the ego, and the intellect is *vaikṛta*; and for one who does not know the principle of the Puruṣa and performs only sacrifices and charitable works (*iṣṭāpūrta*), it is *dākṣiṇa*. Thus, among these three types [of devotion], there is bondage due to the absence of knowledge of the true nature of the Puruṣa. 20.
Now, one might ask: upon the cessation of these three types of ignorance, what kind of liberation arises? To this he says:
"Liberation is threefold. (Tattvasaṃgraha 21)

For one who perceives the worthlessness of rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta* and recognizes that the realization of the true nature of the Person (*puruṣa*) alone is the essence, there is the first [stage]. Then, for one who understands the state of being a modification (*vikāratā*) even regarding the elements and the senses, and subsequently knows the Self as distinct from them, there is the second. The third consists of the form of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Although the first and second are not ultimate liberations, they should nevertheless be understood as being designated as "liberation" because bondage is removed to a certain extent through the renunciation of the notion of identity with those [levels].

In this context, bondage, liberation, and saṃsāra belong to primordial nature (prakṛti) alone and not to the person (puruṣa), because these are impossible in the person, who is unchanging and devoid of the latent impressions of afflictions and karmic residues. Thus, just as the victory or defeat of servants is metaphorically attributed to the master, so too the bondage and other states residing in primordial nature are metaphorically attributed to the person; and in this way, the connection of the person with experience and liberation—even though they reside in primordial nature—is well-established through the non-apprehension of their distinction.

And thus, through these seven forms—namely, knowledge and ignorance of the *dharma*s, detachment and non-detachment, and sovereignty and lack of sovereignty—*prakṛti* binds the self for the sake of the *puruṣa*'s purpose, which consists of experience and liberation; yet, by means of one form, namely discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) arising from the knowledge of reality, she liberates it.
Through the practice of such knowledge of reality—cultivated with reverence, continuity, and over a long period—one attains the direct perception of the distinctness between *sattva* and *puruṣa*.

Kevala-jñāna arises, by which even the beginningless latent impression of error (viparyaya-vāsanā) is obstructed; consequently, all internal operations—namely determination, conceit, volition, and perception—as well as all external activities, are prohibited within the Self. This alone is liberation; such is the established doctrine. // 21 //

Now, one might ask: how can worldly people effect the experience of all objects of knowledge—both those that are unmanifest, such as the Puruṣa and Prakṛti, and those that are manifest, such as jars and cloth?
To this, he says: "The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is threefold. (TS 22)

Valid cognition (*pramā*) is a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) whose object is indubitable, non-erroneous, and not already known, as well as the corresponding spiritual awareness (*pauruṣeyabodha*). The instrument (*karaṇa*) of that valid cognition is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). It is of three kinds, distinguished as perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and verbal testimony (*śabda*).

By this, the additional means of knowledge such as comparison (*upamāna*) accepted by the Naiyāyikas and others are included within these very categories; thus, they do not function as separate [instruments].
In this context, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the sense faculty in proximity to its object;
inference (*anumāna*) is preceded by the knowledge of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*);
and verbal testimony (*śabda*) arises from the words of a reliable authority (*āptavacana*), such as the Vedas and so forth.
In particular, their definitions and illustrations should be understood from the original source; may there be auspiciousness! 22.

Since that [Prakṛti], though one, is born as twofold through its union with the principle of the three guṇas, it thus attains duality and spontaneously and incessantly manifests both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
may this pair of pairs of stainless Sūtras of Kapila, which thus clearly indicates the removal of the delusion of the wise, long endure in the hearts of the intelligent.
Thus ends the *Sarvopakāriṇī*, a concise commentary on the *Kāpila-sūtra*.
